pages.wrong_reason: False as stated. A polynomial commitment with $O(1)$-size evaluation proofs does not by itself yield a succinct NIZK for NP in the standard model: (a) compiling a polynomial IOP with a PCS gives an interactive argument, and non-interactivity needs Fiat-Shamir in the ROM or a structured setup, neither supplied by a PCS; (b) zero knowledge needs a hiding PCS with zero-knowledge evaluation proofs, which evaluation binding does not supply; (c) knowledge soundness needs extractability, not evaluation binding. The true theorem - an extractable hiding PCS yields a zkSNARK for NP in the ROM via polynomial-IOP compilation (CHMMVW20, EUROCRYPT 2020, eprint 2019/1047; BFS20, EUROCRYPT 2020, eprint 2019/1229) - is the red-pcs-to-snark edge with its qualifiers. The migration's SUSPECTED MATHEMATICAL ERROR flag is correct.

sources.ref_file_title: BFS20 - Transparent SNARKs from DARK Compilers
sources.authors: Benedikt Bünz, Ben Fisch, Alan Szepieniec
sources.note: cryptobib EC:BunFisSze20, pp. 677-706, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-45721-1_24 (verified in vendor/cryptobib). Abstract (verified via search snippet): compiles polynomial IOPs with a polynomial commitment scheme into public-coin interactive arguments of knowledge for any NP relation with succinct communication; zk via a hiding PCS with zero-knowledge evaluations; SNARKs via Fiat-Shamir. Concurrent with CHMMVW20.

pages.class_justification: The compiled construction uses the PCS as a black box, but knowledge soundness invokes the PCS extractor (an extractability property, not oracle access to an adversary) and non-interactivity uses Fiat-Shamir in the ROM; neither source places the compilation in the RTV04 taxonomy.
pages.model_justification: The PIOP-with-PCS compilation yields a public-coin interactive argument in the standard model; both sources obtain the non-interactive SNARK by Fiat-Shamir in the random-oracle model. The PCS's setup carries over: a transparent PCS gives a transparent SNARK, a structured-setup PCS (e.g. KZG) gives a universal-SRS preprocessing SNARK.
pages.statement: Any extractable [[polynomial-commitment|PCS]] with succinct commitments and evaluation proofs yields a preprocessing [[succinct-argument|SNARK]] for NP in the random-oracle model: the prover of a polynomial IOP for NP (an unconditional object) commits to each round's polynomials and answers the verifier's evaluation queries with evaluation proofs, and Fiat–Shamir makes the resulting public-coin argument non-interactive [[CHMMVW20 - Marlin Preprocessing zkSNARKs with Universal and Updatable SRS|CHMMVW20]], [[BFS20 - Transparent SNARKs from DARK Compilers|BFS20]]. The PCS's setup carries over — a transparent PCS yields a transparent SNARK — and a hiding PCS with zero-knowledge evaluation proofs yields a zkSNARK.
pages.sketch: Each oracle the PIOP prover would send becomes a PCS commitment and each verifier query an evaluation opening. For knowledge soundness, the PCS extractor recovers the committed polynomials from a convincing prover; these define a PIOP prover from which the PIOP extractor recovers a witness.

pages.class_justification: The VC algorithms call the PCS only as an oracle (interpolation over fixed points is public preprocessing), and a position-binding adversary's output — two accepting openings of different values at position $i$ — is verbatim an evaluation-binding break at the point $\omega_i$, so the reduction runs the adversary once as an oracle and forwards its output. Fixed construction, fixed reduction: the RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: A [[polynomial-commitment|PCS]] over $\FF$ for degree bound $n-1$, with $n \le |\FF|$, yields a [[commitment-scheme#vector-commitments|vector commitment]] for $\FF^n$: fix distinct $\omega_1, \dots, \omega_n \in \FF$, commit to $(v_1, \dots, v_n)$ as a commitment to the polynomial $f$ of degree $< n$ with $f(\omega_i) = v_i$, and open position $i$ with an evaluation proof for $f(\omega_i) = v_i$. Position binding is evaluation binding at $\omega_i$ — folklore.
pages.sketch: Interpolation turns the vector into a polynomial; a position opening is an evaluation proof at the fixed point $\omega_i$, and two conflicting openings of position $i$ are two conflicting evaluation proofs at $\omega_i$.

sources.authors: Christian Cachin, Silvio Micali, Markus Stadler

sources.ref_file_title: GR05 - Single-Database Private Information Retrieval with Constant Communication Rate
sources.note: cryptobib ICALP:GenRam05, pp. 803-815, DOI 10.1007/11523468_65 (verified in vendor/cryptobib). Constant communication rate single-database PIR; per its abstract (search snippet) the composite-modulus instantiation rests on 'a simple variant of the Phi-hiding assumption'.

pages.class_justification: Assumption-to-primitive construction; CMS99 do not classify the reduction in RTV04 terms and the taxonomy is defined for primitive-to-primitive reductions, so `unstated` is the honest value.
pages.model_justification: The CMS99 scheme is in the standard model: privacy reduces to Φ-hiding, correctness is unconditional.
pages.statement: Under the [[rsa-assumption#-hiding|Φ-hiding]] assumption, introduced in the same work, there is a single-server [[single-server-private-information-retrieval|cPIR]] scheme with total communication polylogarithmic in the database size $n$ [[CMS99 - Computationally Private Information Retrieval with Polylogarithmic Communication|CMS99]].
pages.sketch: The client derives a prime $p_i$ from index $i$ via a shared prime-sequence generator, sends a modulus $m$ with $p_i \mid \phi(m)$ — which by Φ-hiding hides $p_i$ — and a $p_i$-th non-residue $x \in \ZZ_m^*$. The server returns $x^e \bmod m$ for $e = \prod_j p_j^{b_j}$; knowing the factorization of $m$, the client tests whether the reply is a $p_i$-th residue, which holds iff $b_i = 1$.
pages.improvements_text: - A variant of Φ-hiding yields single-database PIR with constant communication rate — [[GR05 - Single-Database Private Information Retrieval with Constant Communication Rate|GR05]].

sources.ref_file_title: HILL99 - A Pseudorandom Generator from Any One-Way Function
sources.authors: Johan Håstad, Russell Impagliazzo, Leonid A. Levin, Michael Luby
sources.note: Cited in improvements_text for the generic OWF -> PRG step avoiding the perfect-correctness caveat.
Cited in improvements_text: statistically binding two-message commitment from any PRG.

pages.class_justification: The commitment algorithms call $\KeyGen$ and $\Enc$ only as oracles; the hiding reduction runs any commitment distinguisher as an oracle and is a CPA adversary with the same advantage; binding is information-theoretic given perfect correctness and a well-formed key, so no reduction is needed there. Fixed construction, fixed reduction: the RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: Committing to $m$ as $(\pk, c)$ with $(\sk, \pk) \gets \KeyGen(1^\secpar)$ and $c \gets \Enc(\pk, m; r)$, and opening by revealing $(m, r)$, turns any perfectly correct CPA-secure [[public-key-encryption|PKE]] into a non-interactive [[commitment-scheme|commitment]]: hiding reduces tightly to CPA security, and binding holds because perfect correctness makes $c$ determine the plaintext — openings $(m_0, r_0), (m_1, r_1)$ of $c$ with $m_0 \ne m_1$ would force $\Dec(\sk, c)$ to equal both. This binding argument covers only $\pk$ in the support of $\KeyGen$; a malicious committer may choose a malformed $\pk$ unless keys are certifiable — folklore.
pages.improvements_text: - Without perfect correctness or certifiable keys, PKE still yields commitments: PKE implies a one-way function, hence a [[pseudorandom-generator|PRG]] [[HILL99 - A Pseudorandom Generator from Any One-Way Function|HILL99]], hence a two-message statistically binding commitment [[Naor91 - Bit commitment using pseudorandomness|Naor91]].

sources.ref_file_title: IL89 - One-way Functions are Essential for Complexity Based Cryptography
sources.note: cryptobib FOCS:ImpLub89, pp. 230-235, DOI 10.1109/SFCS.1989.63483 (verified in vendor/cryptobib). Canonical citation for 'private-key encryption, identification, commitment and coin flipping imply one-way functions' (confirmed via search snippets); PKE is subsumed via PKE => SKE.

pages.class_justification: The one-way function is computed by running the PKE algorithms as oracles (e.g. mapping key-generation randomness to the public key), and the reduction runs any inverter as an oracle to obtain a secret key consistent with $\pk$ and decrypt the CPA challenge. Fixed construction, fixed reduction.
pages.statement: Any CPA-secure [[public-key-encryption|PKE]] implies a [[hash-function#preimage-resistance-one-wayness|one-way function]] [[IL89 - One-way Functions are Essential for Complexity Based Cryptography|IL89]], an instance of the theorem that private-key encryption, identification, commitment and coin flipping each require one-way functions.
pages.sketch: For a perfectly correct scheme, $f(r) := \pk$ where $(\sk, \pk) = \KeyGen(1^\secpar; r)$ is one-way: an inverter returns $r'$ with $\KeyGen(1^\secpar; r') = (\sk', \pk)$, and perfect correctness makes $\sk'$ decrypt every ciphertext under $\pk$, so the reduction decrypts the CPA challenge. IL89's general argument uses distributional inverters and does not need perfect correctness.

pages.class_justification: The protocol runs $\KeyGen$ and $\Enc$ as oracles; the reduction embeds its CPA challenge $(\pk, c^*)$ as the transcript and runs any eavesdropper on it as an oracle, turning a key-vs-uniform distinguisher into a CPA distinguisher with the same advantage. pages.statement: Any CPA-secure [[public-key-encryption|PKE]] yields a two-message [[key-exchange|KE]] protocol secure against eavesdroppers: $B$ sends $\pk$ from $(\sk, \pk) \gets \KeyGen(1^\secpar)$, $A$ replies with $c \gets \Enc(\pk, k)$ for $k \getsr \calK \subseteq \calM$, and both output $k$. sources.ref_file_title: CS03 - Design and Analysis of Practical Public-Key Encryption Schemes Secure against Adaptive Chosen Ciphertext Attack
sources.note: cryptobib CraSho03 (SIAM J. Comput. 33(1), pp. 167-226) and EPRINT:CraSho01b (verified in vendor/cryptobib; venue confirmed via search snippet). Formalizes the KEM abstraction and the KEM/DEM hybrid framework; the standard citable form of this folklore transformation.

pages.class_justification: $\mathsf{Encap}$ and $\mathsf{Decap}$ call $\Enc$ and $\Dec$ only as oracles, and the reduction runs any KEM adversary as an oracle, forwarding its decapsulation queries to the decryption oracle with a challenge embedding fixed in advance. pages.statement: Any IND-CCA [[public-key-encryption|PKE]] whose message space contains the key space $\calK$ yields an IND-CCA [[key-encapsulation-mechanism|KEM]]: $\mathsf{Encap}(\pk)$ samples $k \getsr \calK$ and outputs $(\Enc(\pk, k), k)$; $\mathsf{Decap}(\sk, c) := \Dec(\sk, c)$. The KEM game maps query-for-query onto the PKE game — folklore.
pages.sketch: The reduction picks independent uniform $k_0, k_1 \getsr \calK$, submits them as its PKE challenge pair, hands the KEM adversary $(\pk, c^*, k_0)$, and answers decapsulation queries with its decryption oracle; when $c^*$ encrypts $k_1$, the shown key $k_0$ is independent of $c^*$, which is the KEM's random-key world.

pages.wrong_reason: Not a theorem as stated: OT is not known to follow from generic PKE. GKM+00 (FOCS 2000; existing wiki reference 'GKM+00 - The relationship between public key encryption and oblivious transfer'; existing barrier page no-pke-to-ot-gkm-00) prove PKE and OT incomparable under black-box reductions by an IR89-style oracle separation, which rules out relativizing and hence every fully-black-box construction; no non-black-box construction is known.
